one_liner: Zig fork/join library using heartbeat scheduling; sub-nanosecond fork/join overhead versus Rayon's ~15 ns per join.
what_it_does: Spice is a ~500-line Zig module that gives fork/join parallelism over recursive code. Every parallel function takes a *spice.Task, recursive calls go through t.call, and a Future is forked, the caller does its own half, then join returns the other half's result or null, in which case the caller runs that work inline. A ThreadPool is started with a background worker count and a heartbeat interval; it is not a drop-in for any C++ pool and has no parallel-for or slice API.
how_it_is_fast: Heartbeat scheduling (Acar, Charguéraud, Rainey): instead of making every fork stealable, a heartbeat thread flips a per-worker atomic flag about every 100 us, and only then does the worker promote its oldest queued fork into a shared job. Between heartbeats a fork is a push onto a branch-free, sentinel-headed intrusive doubly-linked list on the stack with no atomics, and an unclaimed join is a pop plus a direct, inlinable static call, so the code compiles close to the sequential version. The heartbeat path is marked cold so it costs no registers, Task state is passed as function parameters so LLVM keeps it in registers, and coordination uses a single uncontended mutex with condition waits and no spinning.
when_to_use: Recursive divide-and-conquer in Zig (tree walks, quicksort-style recursion) where each leaf does only nanoseconds of work and Rayon-style per-join overhead would dominate.
Code that runs on inputs of unpredictable size: on a 1000-node tree Spice stays at sequential speed instead of slowing down, because nothing gets shared before the first heartbeat.
Shared or busy machines where you want idle worker threads to sleep rather than spin.
As a reference design for building a low-overhead heartbeat scheduler in C or C++; the whole runtime is one readable file under 0BSD.
when_not_to_use: Production or safety-critical code: the author calls it a research project with zero test coverage, heavy use of @panic for errors, and no plans for active development.
Large coarse-grained workloads that need the best scaling: Rayon scaled 14x at 16 threads against Spice's 11x, because each worker shares at most one job per heartbeat.
Data-parallel loops over arrays or slices: there is no parallel-for or iterator API, only fork/join on recursive functions.
Mixes of slow and fast tasks: open issue #10 describes how a thread waiting on a stolen slow job is not woken for new work, so the pool can degenerate.
C++ projects that need a native library: it is Zig-only with no C ABI layer, so use from C++ means writing and exporting your own wrapper.

integration.dependencies: none for the library (parg is a lazy dependency only for the example)
integration.min_toolchain: Current HEAD targets Zig 0.16.0-dev (uses std.Io; last commit supports 0.16.0-dev.2915); the published benchmark used commit 0b697d6 on Zig 0.14.0-dev.564
integration.platforms: any target Zig's std.Thread supports; benchmarked only on x86-64 Linux (and an M3 Pro anecdote)
integration.thread_safety: Pool is shared across threads via one internal mutex; ThreadPool.call creates a one-off worker per caller. Task and Future values are per-thread and must not be shared.

gotchas: Every fork must be followed by join or tryJoin, and a null result from join means you must run the work yourself; misuse is not checked and the README warns that 'weird things could happen'.
A forked function's result is limited to 32 bytes (4 u64 words); larger return types are a compile error.

Finding a ready job is an O(workers) scan under the global mutex (open issue #8), and the heartbeat thread visits workers round-robin, so each worker's effective heartbeat interval stays near 100 us however many workers there are.
The code tracks Zig dev releases (std.Io API), so it breaks across Zig versions; pin a commit that matches your compiler.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Spice over chili (its Rust port) only if you write Zig or want the original reference code; pick it over Fork Union or citor only for fine-grained recursive fork/join, since those are C++ libraries with parallel-for APIs and broader benchmarks. For C++ heartbeat scheduling the deepsea-inria/heartbeat prototype is the closest catalogued sibling.
verified_claims_summary: Author's single make bench run (August 2024, commit 0b697d6, Zig 0.14.0-dev ReleaseFast versus rustc 1.77.2 with Criterion) on a Google Cloud c4-standard-16 (16 vCPUs, CPU model not stated): summing a 100M-node balanced tree took 3.93 ns/node with Spice on 1 thread against a 3.63 ns Zig baseline, and 0.36 ns at 16 threads; Rayon took 22.99 ns on 1 thread against a 7.48 ns Rust baseline, and 1.64 ns at 16 threads. On a 1000-node tree Rayon became about 60x slower than its baseline at 32 threads while Spice stayed flat. Each library is compared with its own language's baseline, and those baselines differ by 2x.
status_note: Described by the author as a research project with no active feature work, but commits through 2026-03-22 keep it building on Zig 0.16-dev; 0BSD and about 500 lines, so easy to vendor or port.
